items.title: The Sixteenth and Final Doctrine: Reading Fortune in the Stars

items.zh: 妄計吉祥論者，謂如有一，若沙門、若婆羅門，起如是見，立如是論：若世間日月薄蝕，星宿失度，所欲為事皆不成就；若彼隨順，所欲皆成。為此義故，精勤供養日月星等，祠火誦呪，安置茅草，滿瓫頻螺果及餉佉等。
items.en: The doctrine of false auspiciousness: there are certain renunciants or brahmins who hold such a view and establish such a doctrine — that when the sun or moon is eclipsed, or the stars fall out of their proper course, no desired undertaking whatsoever can succeed; but when these bodies move favourably, every desired thing succeeds. For this reason, they diligently make offerings to the sun, moon, and stars, tend sacred fires, recite incantations, scatter sacred grass, and fill jars with bilva fruit and conch shells.

items.zh: 謂曆算者作如是計。問：彼何因緣，起如是見，立如是論？答：由教及理故。教如前說。理者，謂如有一，為性尋思，乃至廣說。
彼由獲得世間靜慮，世間皆謂是阿羅漢。若有欲得自身富樂，所祈果遂者，便往請問。然彼不如實知業果相應緣生道理，但見世間日月薄蝕、星度行時，爾時眾生淨不淨業果報成熟，彼則計為日月等作。復為信樂此事者建立顯說。
items.en: Having attained worldly meditative concentration, such teachers are widely regarded by the world as arhats, and anyone wishing for their own wealth and happiness, or for a wish to be fulfilled, comes to consult them. Yet they do not genuinely understand the true workings of karmic result and dependent origination; they merely observe that, at the time an eclipse or irregular planetary motion occurs, beings' pure or impure karma also happens to ripen — and from this, they conclude that the sun, moon, and stars themselves are the cause. They then elaborate and proclaim this teaching for the benefit of those inclined to believe it.

items.title: The Final Refutation, and All Sixteen Doctrines Are Declared Unreasoned

items.zh: 今應問彼，汝何所欲？世間興衰等事，為是日月薄蝕星度等作？為淨不淨業所作耶？若言日等作者，現見盡壽隨造福非福業，感此興衰苦樂等果，不應道理。若淨不淨業所作者，計日等作，不應道理。如是日等作故，淨不淨業作故，不應道理。是故此論非如理說。
items.en: One should press them: what do you actually intend — is the world's rise and fall brought about by eclipses and irregular planetary motion, or by pure and impure karma? If by the sun and the rest, then the plainly observed fact that people, throughout their lives, bring about their own rise, fall, pleasure, and pain according to whether they perform meritorious or demeritorious deeds makes no sense on your account. If by pure and impure karma, then attributing this instead to the sun and the rest makes no sense. Therefore, this doctrine is not a soundly reasoned teaching.

items.zh: 如是十六種異論，由二種門發起觀察，由正道理推逐觀察，於一切種皆不應理。
items.en: Thus, these sixteen divergent doctrines, examined through two gateways of inquiry and pursued through sound reasoning, are found, in every single case, to not accord with reason.

blocks.text: The last and shortest reading of fascicle 7: the sixteenth doctrine, that fortune depends on the stars, and the treatise's verdict on all sixteen. Use the extra time to review the list of sixteen; together they make a map of the ways the mind goes wrong when it reasons without wisdom.
Untranslated (0312c23–c25): "It is the calendar-reckoners (astrologers) who hold this. Why do they hold this view?"

The sixteenth doctrine: "When the sun or moon is eclipsed, or the stars fall out of their proper course, no desired undertaking can succeed; but when these bodies move favourably, every undertaking succeeds." So its followers worship the heavens, tend sacred fires, chant, lay out grass, and set out bilva fruit and conch shells. Master Cháng Bǎi explains the objects: grass at home keeps spirits away; the bilva is a red fruit; the conch is a lucky shell. (Compare Day 31's "resources of good omen".)

How does the view arise? Its teachers have attained worldly concentration and are "widely regarded by the world as arhats". Not understanding karma and dependent origination, they observe that eclipses coincide with the ripening of karma and credit the heavens. Master Cháng Bǎi: they invert the relation. The world, sun and moon included, arises from beings' shared karma (Day 8); "they think sun and moon are primary and people secondary".

"Is the world's rise and fall brought about by eclipses and irregular planetary motion, or by pure and impure karma?" If by the heavens, then people's lifelong deeds would have nothing to do with their fortune, which contradicts experience. If by karma, crediting the heavens makes no sense. Master Cháng Bǎi: "practising merit such as the five precepts and ten good deeds, or demerit like the ten evils, brings prosperity, decline, pain, or joy."

"These sixteen divergent doctrines, examined through two gateways of inquiry and pursued through sound reasoning, are found, in every single case, to not accord with reason." Master Cháng Bǎi gives two readings of "two gateways": the *Yujia lunji* takes them as scripture and reasoning; the *Pīxún jì* as the two opposite options posed in each dilemma. He also explains the method word 徵詰: 徵 is asking in detail; 詰 is pressing further until the position's unreasonableness is plain.

subs.head: Looking back on the sixteen doctrines

items: **About causation:** effect pre-existing in the cause; manifestation; no cause; a creator; past deeds alone; the stars.
**About time and self:** real past and future; a self; permanence; annihilation; the world bounded or boundless.
**About the moral and spiritual life:** killing as duty; caste supremacy; false purity; evasive teaching; nihilism about karma and about all characteristics.

blocks.text: Against each the treatise sets the same few principles: things arise from causes and conditions; causes are impermanent; the self is a convenient designation on the aggregates; karma is carried as present seeds and ripens over many lives; and the three natures must be distinguished, so that emptiness is not mistaken for nothing.
This completes the fourth gateway of the three grounds of thought. Fascicle 8 takes up the fifth: defilement and its arising.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what does the doctrine of false auspiciousness claim?
options: when sun or moon is eclipsed or stars stray, nothing succeeds; when they're favourable, all does — so they worship the heavens, tend fires, chant, lay grass, and fill jars with bilva fruit and conch
quiz.why: "When the sun or moon is eclipsed, or the stars fall out of their proper course, no desired undertaking whatsoever can succeed; but when these bodies move favourably, every desired thing succeeds. For this reason, they diligently make offerings to the sun, moon, and stars, tend sacred fires, recite incantations, scatter sacred grass, and fill jars with bilva fruit and conch shells." A is the treatise's own view.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, how do these teachers come to their view?
options: having worldly absorption, they're taken for arhats; not understanding karma and dependent origination, they see eclipses coincide with karma ripening and credit the heavens
quiz.why: "Having attained worldly meditative concentration, such teachers are widely regarded by the world as arhats … they merely observe that, at the time an eclipse or irregular planetary motion occurs, beings' pure or impure karma also happens to ripen — and from this, they conclude that the sun, moon, and stars themselves are the cause." Coincidence taken for cause. Venerable Miào Jìng: "This person is deceiving people."

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain the real relation between the heavens and karma, and where sun- and moon-worship came from?
options: the karmic body is the ripened result; the world arises through shared karma's dominant force — outsiders invert it, making the heavens primary and people secondary, hence fire- and sun-worship
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The result-body is the ripened result; by shared karma's dominant force, the world beings need arises"; "they think sun and moon are primary and people secondary, so they worship sun and moon — fire cults and sun cults." Sun and moon arise from beings' shared karma; they don't rule it.

quiz.q: How does the treatise refute false auspiciousness?
options: is the world's rise and fall caused by eclipses or by pure and impure karma? If eclipses, people's lifelong deeds bringing their fortunes makes no sense; if karma, crediting the heavens makes no sense
quiz.why: "Is the world's rise and fall brought about by eclipses and irregular planetary motion, or by pure and impure karma?" Master Cháng Bǎi: throughout life, merit like the five precepts and ten good deeds, or demerit like the ten evils, brings rise, fall, pain, and pleasure. Venerable Miào Jìng: Buddhism teaches we reap what we sow; if the heavens ruled, we could only sit and wait.

quiz.q: "Pursued through sound reasoning" — how does Master Cháng Bǎi, per the Pixunji, distinguish 徵 and 詰?
options: 徵 is detailed questioning; 詰 is pressing further, rebuking the opponent's position as unreasonable
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "徵 is asking in detail; 詰 is pressing further, rebuking the other side as unreasonable — that is 'pursuing through sound reasoning.'" Every "What do you intend? … makes no sense" in fascicles 6–7 is this pattern.

quiz.q: What is the treatise's final verdict on the sixteen doctrines?
options: examined through two gateways and pursued through sound reasoning, in every case they fail to accord with reason
quiz.why: "Thus, these sixteen divergent doctrines, examined through two gateways of inquiry and pursued through sound reasoning, are found, in every single case, to not accord with reason." This closes the establishment of unsound attention; fascicle 8 opens the fifth gateway, how defilement arises.

quiz.q: According to Master Cháng Bǎi, what truly brings about the world's rise and fall, pain and pleasure?
options: lifelong deeds — merit like the five precepts and ten good deeds, or demerit like the ten evils — bring rise, fall, pain, or joy
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Practising merit such as the five precepts and ten good deeds, or demerit like the ten evils, brings prosperity, decline, pain, or joy." The text: people "throughout their lives, bring about their own rise, fall, pleasure, and pain." It echoes §4: suffering has past, mixed, and present causes — none apart from karma.
